faqs.q: How long does a dental filling last?
faqs.a: It depends on the material, the size and position of the filling, and how well you look after your teeth. Amalgam and ceramic fillings generally last longer than composite or glass ionomer fillings, but any filling can eventually need replacing because of wear or new decay, so regular check-ups help catch problems early.

Amalgam fillings contain mercury, but major dental bodies consider them safe for most people. If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, getting a filling for a young child or simply prefer to avoid mercury, ask your dentist about tooth-coloured alternatives such as composite or glass ionomer fillings.

faqs.q: Does getting a dental filling hurt?
faqs.a: Getting a filling usually causes little discomfort, because the dentist numbs the area with a local anaesthetic before removing the decay. Mild sensitivity to hot, cold or biting for a few days afterwards is common; if it lasts longer or your bite feels uneven, go back to your dentist.

faqs.q: How soon can I eat after getting a filling?
faqs.a: You can usually eat once the numbness wears off, which helps you avoid biting your cheek or tongue. Tooth-coloured composite fillings are hardened with a special light during the appointment, while silver amalgam fillings take longer to set fully, so your dentist may advise chewing on the other side for a while.
